headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress make prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default; Authelia’s auth outputs can be consumed by LangGraph workflows.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Authelia exposes OIDC/OAuth2 and ForwardAuth outputs, while LangGraph can read/write application files and wire developer-defined tools into graphs. A shared filesystem or stdout/stderr bridge could let attacker-controlled auth content influence downstream prompts. This is not proven by direct integration, but the interaction is plausible in default orchestration.
conditions: IF Authelia output is copied into a LangGraph prompt or tool input without sanitization
IF both agents share a workspace or log stream that LangGraph parses as instructions
mitigations: Add strict prompt delimiters and content escaping
Route Authelia outputs through a schema validator
Disable automatic ingestion of logs into prompts
Use separate workspaces for auth and orchestration
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: LangGraph can read and write application-defined files and sends data to model providers and developer-defined tools; Authelia has broad network egress and handles OIDC/OAuth2 flows. If they share a workspace or secrets-bearing state, LangGraph may expose file contents to third parties. Authelia itself is not shown touching sensitive data, so this is a shared-workspace leakage risk rather than a confirmed exfiltration path.
conditions: IF both agents share a filesystem or checkpointer store containing secrets
IF LangGraph forwards file contents or state to model providers or tools
mitigations: Separate secrets from shared graph state
Restrict LangGraph file access to a dedicated directory
Redact sensitive fields before tool calls
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Authelia has broad network egress and OAuth/OIDC-facing behavior, while LangGraph can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write files. Even without explicit git access, overlapping write and network authority on shared resources can cause race conditions or conflicting side effects in the same deployment. The profiles do not prove a lock manager, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same mutable directory or service endpoint
IF LangGraph nodes invoke shell or subprocess actions while Authelia is serving requests
mitigations: Assign separate service accounts
Use per-agent directories and ports
Serialize writes with an external lock
Disable shell nodes unless required
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination for shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: Authelia can emit authentication decisions via OIDC/OAuth2 and ForwardAuth, and LangGraph is explicitly a stateful orchestration layer that can route outputs into downstream tools. If LangGraph treats Authelia results as authoritative without verification, a mistaken auth decision can cascade into irreversible actions or access grants. This interaction is plausible from the profiles alone, so the safer high severity applies.
conditions: IF LangGraph uses Authelia responses as direct triggers for tool execution
IF no verification step checks auth claims before downstream actions
mitigations: Insert a verification step before acting on auth results
Require human approval for privileged branches
Log and diff auth claims against policy
Limit downstream tools to read-only until verified
requires-engineering: implement policy-as-code gating

E_compliance.rationale: Authelia is an authentication layer with no stated data-class handling, while LangGraph explicitly handles model-provider API keys and application-defined graph state with persistent checkpointer storage. If regulated identity data or secrets are placed into that shared state, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not show a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated identity data is stored in LangGraph checkpointer state
IF retention or deletion requirements apply to the shared graph store
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of graph state
Set explicit retention limits on the checkpointer
Document deletion/export procedures
Store secrets in a separate vault
requires-engineering: add residency-aware storage controls
